sections.history: Tirumundeeswaram, known today by the name of its village, Gramam, in Villupuram district, is a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nadu Nadu country, sung in the Tevaram by the saint Tirunavukkarasar, Appar, in a decad of the Sixth Tirumurai. Tradition holds that Appar performed uzhavarappani here, the humble service of cleaning and tending the temple grounds, as an act of devotion. Inscriptions record the village under the old name Mouli-gramam in the days of the Chola king Parantaka I, and tell that the older Shiva temple was rebuilt in stone in about 943 CE by Vellangumaran, a general from Kerala who served the prince Rajaditya, whose army was then stationed at Gramam. Inscriptions of earlier years appear to have been engraved again on the new walls.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and rises behind a tall entrance gopuram. It covers about an acre, with its shrines enclosed within large concentric rectangular walls of granite, in the Dravidian manner. In the sanctum Shivaloka Nathar is worshipped as a linga, and the goddess Soundaranayaki has her own shrine. Beside the temple lies its sacred tank, the Brahma Theertham, also called the Mundaka Theertham. Students of Chola architecture place the temple's plain, restrained forms in the earliest Chola period, which gives it a quiet, archaic character.
sections.legends: Two traditions account for the name Mundeeswarar. The first traces it to Tindi and Mundi, the guardian attendants of Shiva, who are said to have worshipped the Lord here. The second tells of a king who discovered a Shiva linga within a lotus in the temple's pond; when his arrow struck the flower, it is said to have bled and turned the water crimson, and the place was held sacred thereafter. And the memory of Appar, who gave humble labour to the shrine, is counted among the temple's own stories: the great saint who came to sing and stayed to sweep.
sections.festivals: The temple's most prominent festivals are Chitra Pournami, in the Tamil month of Chithirai (April–May), and Aani Thirumanjanam, the great anointing of the Lord in Aani (June–July). Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March) and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirumundeeswaram is a place for a quiet country pilgrimage. Pass through the gopuram, make your way to the sanctum of Shivaloka Nathar, and then to the shrine of the goddess Soundaranayaki. Walk beside the sacred tank, and remember Appar, who gave to this temple not only his hymns but his labour. Set in a village of Villupuram district rather than a busy town, the temple holds an old, rural calm, and its plain granite walls reward those who linger.

visit.timings: Typically open in the early morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a long break at midday; sources differ on the exact hours, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the village of Gramam, about 16 km from Villupuram on the Arasur–Ulundurpettai road, and the Gramam bus stop is close to the temple. Regular buses run from Villupuram, and buses from Tirukoilur via Arasur also stop at Gramam. Villupuram Junction is the main railway station for the journey.
